text:
The Economics Behind the Norman Conquest: Who Actually Got Paid to Invade England?

William the Conqueror didn't have a payroll for Hastings. No invoice for the fleet. No daily wage table for the army. So how did an invasion actually get financed — and who really profited when it succeeded?

This episode follows the money from the Norman coast to the Domesday Book. We trace the Ship List that put 776 vessels into William's fleet, the magnates who bankrolled their own transport and followers, the treasure and tribute that flowed the moment the crown was won, and the tax system William inherited rather than built.

Then we follow one man's ledger from start to finish: Robert of Mortain, credited with the largest single contribution in the Ship List — 120 ships. Twenty years later, Domesday Book shows him holding roughly 797 manors, 248 of them in Cornwall alone. What happened in between — rebellion, castle-building, garrison costs, and the political risk of falling out of favor — is the real story of how conquest turns into wealth.

By 1086, England's royal demesne had nearly doubled in value while the old English landholding elite had been reduced to a fraction of the country's wealth. This is the P&L of 1066: what it cost to invade, what it paid to win, and why the biggest fortunes weren't made in cash.

Medieval bakers did not always have the freedom to simply raise the price of bread when their costs went up. Wheat could become more expensive, workers still had to be paid, ovens still needed fuel, and officials could punish bakers who sold loaves below the required weight.

So how did a bakery actually stay profitable?

This video explores how the medieval English bread assize worked, why the same coin could buy different amounts of bread depending on grain prices, how the rules accounted for costs like wood, labour, salt and preparation, and where the baker’s own gain was supposed to come from.

We also look at real cases involving underweight bread, confiscations, customer-supplied dough, cash-flow pressure, and the difference between a legally smaller loaf and outright fraud.

The medieval bakery was not just a shop selling bread. It was a tightly regulated business trying to balance grain prices, production costs, customer demand, and the law.

Everyone went looking for Templar gold. They were digging in the wrong place.

There is a barn in Essex, built around 1220, that outlasted the entire order.
It is the oldest thing the Knights Templar left behind in England — and it is a
better guide to where their money actually came from than any treasure map ever

where the revenue came from, and why an organisation with the largest estate in
England still ran short of cash.

In this episode:
— Why a vow of poverty was an accounting decision, not just a spiritual one
— The 1139 papal privilege that created a tax-exempt multinational with no
  local regulator
— How Bernard of Clairvaux's endorsement worked as the best marketing campaign
  of the 12th century
— Why every new recruit was an acquisition channel, not a hiring cost
— The 1185 Inquest: 17,000+ acres, 20 mills, and 18 churches — in one county
— Wool, fulling mills, market rights, and the sheep that funded the Crusades
— How the letter of credit worked, and why it made carrying gold unnecessary
— Lending to kings: Louis VII, King John's crown jewels, and the Saladin tithe
— How the order lent money at scale without ever committing the sin of usury
— Why the treasury was never the product — and what Philip IV actually found
  when he opened the doors on 13 October 1307

A NOTE ON SOURCES AND CLAIMS
Every claim in this episode is tiered.
VERIFIED: the 1185 Inquest of Geoffrey FitzStephen; the Cressing Temple grants
of 1137 and 1147; dendrochronological dating of the Barley Barn (c.1205–1235)

UNCERTAIN, AND LABELLED AS SUCH IN THE VIDEO: the size of Philip IV's debt, and

Historical currency figures are given in period money first. Modern equivalents

title: The Economics of Medieval Executioner — A Curse You Pass to Your Son
channelDescription: Subscribe to discover the real costs, hidden risks, and surprising economics behind owning essential local businesses.

text:
Everyone assumes the medieval executioner was poor. He wasn't. In some cities he out-earned the lawyers, the priests, and half the guild masters — and he still couldn't buy his way out of what the job did to his family.

This episode opens the executioner's books line by line. The fee per beheading, and why a clean stroke paid better than a botched one. The knacker contracts, the cesspit work, the tax he collected from lepers and prostitutes because execution income alone couldn't feed a household. The apothecary trade on the side, where the man nobody would sit beside in church sold ointments and set bones for the same neighbors who crossed the street to avoid him.

Then the part the ledger can't price. Barred from guilds. Barred from the churchyard. Housed outside the wall by law. No family would marry into his, so executioners married other executioners' daughters, and the trade closed in on itself until it stopped being a job and became a bloodline. His son inherited the tools, the house, the income — and the exile.

A profitable business is not the same thing as a good inheritance. This is what it cost.

This video breaks down the complete economics of owning a gym in 2026, starting with the real startup costs, which range from 50,000 dollars for a lean specialty studio to well over 500,000 dollars for a full-service health club. From there it explains the operating leverage of the membership model, why personal training at 40 to 60 percent gross margin is the real profit engine, and why June kills more gyms than January saves them. It covers the real failure rate, why approximately 50 percent of gyms do not survive five years almost never because of bad fitness programming but almost always because of bad financial planning, and ends with verified profit numbers for two realistic scenarios: a boutique studio and a mid-size independent gym.

The economics behind a medieval toll bridge look simple from the outside. One river, one crossing, a gate, and everybody who wants the far bank pays on the way past.

Then you open the accounts.

London Bridge, 1420 to 1421. Rent taken in: fifty pounds and ten shillings. Tolls taken from everyone who crossed: fifteen shillings and two pence. Same bridge, same twelve months — and the gate everybody pictures brought in a fraction of one percent of what the buildings on top of it did.

That gap is where this episode starts. It is not where it ends.

Because the number I actually went looking for does not exist. What did one of these things sell for? What did a man pay to hold one? I searched every English crossing with surviving accounts — London, Rochester, York — expecting a burnt roll or a missing deed. There is no price anywhere, and the reason is not that the records are damaged. It is that the sale they would have recorded could not legally happen.

So this is the system underneath the toll: who really collected it, who really owned the stonework, where the money went, and why an institution that has been earning since the thirteenth century made almost nobody personally rich.

Told through the people whose names are actually in the books. John Woode, who paid twenty pounds a year for the right to collect the cart toll and keep the surplus. The York bridgemasters, whose job title contained the word "bridge" and whose duties did not include the bridge. And two elected wardens a year, every year, walking into a post they could never sell, never inherit, and never keep a penny of.

Real figures from surviving account rolls. Historical currency only, anchored to what a mason earned that same week. Where the record runs out, I say so instead of filling the gap.

Four people stopped at the same counter in Venice on one afternoon. Only one of them was sick.

A woman spent most of a month's household money on a folded paper packet she couldn't read. A painter's boy came in for blue — a colour that cost more by weight than gold. A steward in good livery bought a great deal and paid for none of it. A fourth man said he had rats. He didn't have rats.

The sick woman was the least profitable person to walk through that door all day.

This is the shop that sold spice, sugar, and the pigment behind Renaissance altarpieces out of the same jars as its medicine — plus a plague-era perfume aristocrats wore against bad air, plus, quietly, an ounce of ground human remains, stocked for decades as a legitimate cure. Grinding made every one of those jars unreadable, and unreadable is exactly what the business was built on. A law from a 13th-century Sicilian king made sure the customer had nowhere else to take that risk but you.

Then it turned around and ate its own trade from the inside, and the sharpest legal case survives from a man who genuinely did not have rats.

Could you actually get rich running one? Only if medicine was never the real business.

Adam atte Hethe died during this accounting year. His copper pot was carried out of his house and sold for two shillings, and the man who took his land paid forty. One tenant dying was worth nearly three times what the entire permanent staff cost for twelve months.

And the manor’s biggest labour supply never appears in the accounts at all—which is exactly why 1349 destroyed the model.

A medieval forge was never the town's weapons store. It was the maintenance department for an entire wooden world.

title: The Economics of A Medieval Bank
channelDescription: Subscribe to discover the real costs, hidden risks, and surprising economics behind owning essential local businesses.

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: Subscribe to discover the real costs, hidden risks, and surprising economics behind owning essential local businesses.

text:
Could you actually get rich owning a medieval bank?

Start with the problem nobody mentions. Lending money at interest was a sin with a name, and the Church's position on it was simple: a usurer sells nothing that belongs to him, only time, and time belongs to God. So the entire business had to be built inside a loophole. It was, and the loophole worked for four hundred years.

The vault is the second lie. In 1427 the Medici bank's Rome office was holding roughly 100,000 florins on deposit from the papal treasury. The total capital of the whole bank — every branch, every partner, everything the owners had actually put in — was about 25,000. One office was sitting on four times the firm's own money, and none of it belonged to them. Giovanni di Bicci had opened the thing in 1397 with 10,000 florins and a table. By his death in 1429 he was worth around 180,000.

The money was never in the lending. It was in the gap between two exchange rates, in two cities, over a fixed three-month period — a loan wearing a currency trade's clothes, and everybody involved knew it. But the branch that actually paid for everything was the one whose largest client had banned the business model in the first place. Between 1420 and 1435, as much as 62 per cent of all Medici profits came out of Rome. That office never even needed capital of its own. It didn't have a fixed address either.

Then the part that kills it, twice. Edward III of England borrowed roughly 900,000 florins from the Bardi and 600,000 from the Peruzzi, defaulted in 1345, and took down the two largest financial houses in Europe. A century and a half later the Medici did it again through a branch manager in Bruges named Tommaso Portinari, who had a contractual ceiling on his lending and ignored it. London closed in 1478 having lost 51,533 florins. Bruges went the same year. Lorenzo de' Medici's written comment on the affair is the driest sentence in Renaissance finance.

Your best customers were always the people you had the least power over. A merchant who doesn't pay can be sued. A king who doesn't pay is still a king.

title: The Economics of Running a Medieval Guild Business

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: Subscribe to discover the real costs, hidden risks, and surprising economics behind owning essential local businesses.

text:
Could you actually get rich owning a medieval guild?

You couldn't own one. Nobody could,  a guild was a corporate body with its own hall, its own seal and a chest of silver, and it belonged to itself. What you could buy was a seat inside it, and that seat was the most expensive thing a working man ever purchased. Seven unpaid years came first; the London heaumers fined a master a hundred shillings in 1347 for binding an apprentice any faster than that. Then the entry fine: fourteen shillings from the shearers of Arras, ten lire from the wool guild of Padua, six shillings and eightpence from the York tailors before you could set up a stall. And in sixteenth-century Paris, the grocers charged a journeyman roughly nine years of wages for a mastership. At a skilled man's sixpence a day, that's fifty-four pounds. Two thousand one hundred and sixty days at the bench.

Then a surviving ledger ruins the story. The books of Andrea Busini and Company, wool merchants of Florence, run from 1556 to 1559: costs of 7,859 florins, profit of 798. Raw wool took 34 per cent of everything they spent. Spinning, weaving and dyeing took most of the rest. General overhead — rent, administration, dues, fines, every institutional charge a guild could possibly level, came to two per cent.

So the fees were never the expensive part. The seat was buying something the fee schedule never mentions: the legal right to be the one who sells. Anyone could spin wool, and half the countryside did. Only a member could put his mark on finished cloth and carry it to market — which is why the men who actually got rich stopped making things and started placing the work across dozens of other people's households. And the guild's own most profitable product was never cloth at all. Mid-eighteenth-century Paris goldsmiths admitted about a quarter of their new masters through purchased "privileges," and fewer than half through the apprenticeship the guild existed to guarantee.

What broke it wasn't the plague, and it wasn't the king. Of Busini's 184 sales, twenty-one were settled in cash. Eleven per cent. Everything else walked out the door on credit, a third of it on twelve-month terms — so a master could be rich in his ledger and empty in his cash box on the same afternoon.

You never owned a medieval guild. For thirty years, a medieval guild owned a small, entirely legal, extremely profitable piece of you.

Could you actually get rich owning a Silk Road caravan, or would it bankrupt you before you reached China?

In this video, we break down the true economics of financing and running a fourteenth-century caravan venture along the Tana-to-Khanbaliq route. From the cargo itself, silver reserves, hired wagons and pack animals, interpreters, tolls, and export duties to the route closures, robbery, and debt that could wipe out a merchant before he ever reached a market.

But silk was only part of the business.

The real money came from moving capital itself: converting goods to silver, silver to paper currency, and paper into Chinese silk at fixed exchange rates, while lending, bill-of-exchange credit, and state trade partnerships ran underneath the whole operation.

In one surviving 1340s merchant manual, the entire outbound journey cost less than two percent of the cargo's value to transport, while the cargo itself could take an ordinary laborer nine hundred years to earn.

Using a real medieval trade manual, documented merchant fortunes, and a reconstructed profit-and-loss model, we examine how much a successful caravan merchant could earn, what could destroy the venture in a single year, and why the most profitable operations on the Silk Road were closer to banks, currency exchanges, and state-backed trading companies than the camel trains people imagine.

Almost every high-speed rail line in the world loses money. Only a handful have ever paid back what they cost to build. So why do governments keep building them?

In this video we break down the real economics. Running the trains can be very profitable; building the track is where the money disappears. We look at the EU auditors' "magic number" of 9 million passengers a year, why Paris–Lyon paid for itself in about a decade, why Spain's huge network has so few passengers, how China State Railway Group ended up with around 6.2 trillion yuan of debt, and why HS2 and California's high-speed rail now cost three to four times their first estimates.

text:
Once you stop thinking of a ship as a vehicle and start thinking of it as a spreadsheet, the answer is simple. This video looks at how a ship's value falls every year until it hits its scrap-steel floor. It covers why owners sell ships for scrap just before their fourth or fifth special survey, and how insurers decide a ship is a "constructive total loss". We also go through the Salem, a supertanker sunk in one of the biggest marine insurance frauds in history, and why removing the Costa Concordia cost almost three times what it took to build. Then there are the ships sunk on purpose, completely legally: artificial reefs like the USS Oriskany, and warships used as SINKEX targets. Last stop is the beaches of Alang, Chittagong and Gadani, where most of the world's old ships end up.

A ship is never worth what it cost to build. It's worth only what it can earn on its next voyage.
